blocks.text: Most of the time you don't build a stack — your language already has one. This lesson shows the built-in stack in each language, the mistakes people make with them, and then how to build your own stack on a linked list so you know exactly what happens underneath.
The built-in stack in each language

blocks.alt: A cheat sheet of stack operations in four languages. JavaScript arrays: push, pop, s[s.length - 1] to peek, length to check empty and size. Python lists: append, pop, s[-1], not s, len(s). Java ArrayDeque: push, pop, peek, isEmpty, size. C++ std::stack: push, pop which returns nothing, top, empty, size.

blocks.text: Here is the same small job in all four: push some values, then pop until the stack is empty. The values come out reversed.

blocks.code:
def pop_all(values):
    stack = []                       # a Python list is the stack
    for x in values:
        stack.append(x)
    out = []
    while stack:                     # an empty list is falsy
        out.append(stack.pop())
    return out                       # [1, 2, 3] -> [3, 2, 1]

items: **Popping or peeking an empty stack.** JavaScript quietly returns `undefined`, Python raises `IndexError`, Java's `pop()` throws, and C++ is undefined behaviour. Check `isEmpty` first whenever the stack might be empty — in loops, write `while (stack is not empty && …)` with the empty check **first**.
**C++ `pop()` returns nothing.** Read `top()` before you call `pop()`.

**Java: prefer `ArrayDeque` over `Stack`.** `java.util.Stack` is an old class built on a synchronised `Vector`; it is slower and lets you reach into the middle. `Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()` with `push`, `pop` and `peek` is the modern choice.
**Python: `pop()`, not `pop(0)`.** `pop(0)` removes from the **front** — that is queue behaviour, and it costs O(n).
**JavaScript: `pop()`, not `shift()`.** `shift()` also removes from the front.

blocks.text: Building a stack on a linked list

A linked list makes a natural stack if you treat its **head** as the **top**. Pushing means adding a node in front of the head; popping means moving the head to the next node. Neither ever walks the list, so both are O(1) — and the stack only stops growing when memory runs out.

blocks.alt: Pushing 30 onto a linked-list stack holding 20 and 10. Step 1: the new node 30 is created and its next arrow points at the current head, 20. Step 2: head moves to 30. Popping reverses this: head moves back to 20.

blocks.alt: A comparison. Array-based stack: items side by side in memory, push is O(1) amortized because the array occasionally doubles, very fast in practice and cache friendly. Linked-list stack: every push is O(1) with no resizing, but each item carries an extra next pointer and lives in its own allocation.

blocks.text: The built-in stacks above are all array-based, and they are the right default. You'll build one yourself in **Stack Implementation using Arrays**, including the doubling trick that makes push O(1) on average.

items: Use the built-in: JavaScript array, Python list, Java `ArrayDeque`, C++ `std::stack`.
Always check for **empty** before pop or peek.
C++ `pop()` returns nothing — read `top()` first. Avoid `java.util.Stack`, `pop(0)` and `shift()`.
A linked list is a stack if its **head is the top**: push and pop only move head.
Array-based stacks are the usual choice; linked stacks never need to resize.
